newsitem.title: USA: Molybdenum pecking order shaken up by Endako sale.
newsitem.headline: Molybdenum pecking order shaken up by Endako sale.

text.p: Thompson Creek soars into third place in the intimate molybdenum pecking order following its planned acquisition of Endako mine from Placer Dome, industry observers said.
"I imagine it will have some kind of effect on the market. You now have consolidation of two primary producers which were two competitors," a rival moly producer official said.
Molybdenum is a key ingredient in special steels.
Late Thursday Placer said it signed a letter of intent to sell Endako in Canada to Thompson Creek of Denver, and Nissho Iwai, of Japan.
Following due diligence, the deal should be closed by May 30 when Thompson will own 75 percent of the mine, and Nissho the balance.
How much Thompson and Nissho will pay for Endako is being kept firmly under wraps.
Moly oxide is currently about $4.50 to $4.70 per pound.
"We believe the cost picture of the two properties will permit us to deal with cycles in molybdenum prices," Thompson Creek's president Steven Mooney told Reuters.
Mooney said it was too soon to provide details of how Endako's material will be sold in future, the latter with its own sales team in Pittsburgh.
"At least for the rest of this year, we don't see any changes. A large percentage (of Endako's output) goes to Japan and we don't see that changing," Mooney said.
Thompson Creek also sells 30 percent of its own output to the Japanese.

Endako produces concentrates, lubricant grade concentrates, and moly oxide, but no ferro-moly. Mooney said there was spare capacity at Thompson Creek's oxide and ferro-moly roaster in Langeloth, Pennsylvania to convert Endako output into ferro-moly.

Mooney said it was too early to say if Langeloth will begin upgrading Endako concentrates in higher value ferro-moly. "Clearly we look for ways to optimise our costs and our product spread," he added.
Earlier this month a conference by Ryan's Notes forecast that moly demand this year would top 238 million pounds, with supply a touch lower at 235 million pounds, the gap filled by stocks.
Cyprus Amax dominates world production with current output at the rate of 64 million pounds a year.
Over half of the world's output is a byproduct of copper production, with Cyprus, Thompson Creek, Endako and Molycorp's recently commissioned Questa mine, the only primary producers in the West.
Such players are referred to as swing producers, and often forced to cut back when prices plunge, as copper producers will continue to churn out molybdenum anyway.

Annual output at Thompson Creek, spun-off from Cyprus Amax in November 1993 to keep anti-trust officials happy, will now rise from 18 million pounds a year to some 32 million pounds when all of Endako's 14 million pounds is included.
This puts the enlarged company in third place behind Cyprus Amax, and Chile's Codelco at 34 million pounds.
Meanwhile one producer source said he was optimistic about the market with demand rising in Europe and the Far East with the U.S. already robust.
"We think demand will be higher in the second half than in the first half. Hopefully that will mean that the Questa material will be absorbed by the market," the producer source said.
